title: Order Types
hook: Know the difference before you touch a chart.

launchpad.outcome: Pick the right order type for the situation, not just recognize the names.
launchpad.missionQuestion: If price never reaches your limit price, does the order fill anyway?

slides.headline: Three orders. Three jobs.
slides.line: Market, limit and stop orders each answer a different question.

cards.label: Market order
cards.sub: Fills immediately at whatever price is available.

cards.label: Limit order
cards.sub: Rests and only fills at your price.

cards.label: Stop order
cards.sub: Sits inactive until triggered, then acts like a market order.

versus.label: Limit order
points: Waits for price to come to you

check.prompt: You think they’re interchangeable, since both “get you into a trade.” Are you right?

options.label: Yes, same result every time
options.feedback: They don’t produce the same result. One chases price, the other waits for it.

options.label: No, it’s speed vs price control
options.why: Right. A market order prioritizes speed, a limit order prioritizes price control. That’s a real trade-off.

slides.headline: Price is at 100. You buy limit at 98.

steps.text: Your order rests at 98. It waits for price to come to you.

check.prompt: If price never trades down to 98, what happens?

options.label: It fills at 100 anyway
options.feedback: That would defeat the purpose of setting a limit price in the first place.

options.label: It never fills
options.why: A limit order only fills at your chosen price or better. There’s no guarantee it fills at all.

options.label: It turns into a market order later
options.feedback: Limit orders don’t auto-convert to market orders just from waiting.

slides.kicker: Pick the order for the job
slides.headline: Protect the long automatically.
slides.line: Exit only if price falls to a level below your entry.

options.label: Limit order
options.feedback: A limit order rests at a price. It doesn’t automatically protect a losing position past a level.

options.label: Market order
options.feedback: A market order fires the instant you place it. It can’t wait to trigger only if price falls to a level.

options.label: Stop order
options.why: Stop orders sit inactive until triggered, exactly what a protective exit needs.

slides.line: I’ll show you later which order types I personally lean on for entries. But market, limit and stop come first, before that preference means anything to you.

slides.prompt: When would you use a stop order instead of a limit order?
slides.modelAnswer: A limit order is for when you want control over your entry price and are willing to risk never getting filled. A stop order is for when you need something to happen automatically once price proves a level, like a protective exit, or an entry that only makes sense once price breaks past a certain point. You reach for a stop order when you need to react to a trigger, not just wait at a price.

takeaways: Market orders trade speed for price control.
Limit orders trade price control for a guaranteed fill.
Stop orders sit inactive until price proves a level, then act like a market order.
remember: Every order type is a trade-off between speed and control.
